Garibaldi damselfish Hypsypops rubicundus is a prominent inhabitant of rocky reefs off the coast of southern California and Baja California, readily identifiable by its striking electric blue body and bright yellow tail. Early in its development, the species hatches from demersal, adhesive eggs after an incubation period of approximately twelve days [ab = approximately twelve days], a developmental interval recorded at a relatively stable seawater temperature of seventeen point five degrees Celsius [T = seventeen point five degrees Celsius]. The newly emerged prolarvae carry a substantial yolk sac and enter an endotrophic phase, gradually absorbing their endogenous reserves before transitioning to active feeding. The initial wet weight at the moment of yolk-sac larval emergence has been estimated at roughly ninety-one millionths of a gram (roughly 91 millionths of a gram) [Wwb = roughly 91 millionths of a gram], a mass that underscores the minute size of the species at the onset of its pelagic larval stage. This remarkably small starting biomass, coupled with the modest incubation duration at that thermal regime, represents a characteristic life history strategy among pomacentrid fishes, which typically produce numerous small offspring to offset high early mortality in the plankton.

As the exogenously feeding larva progresses through its planktonic phase, somatic growth proceeds steadily until the morphological transformation of larval metamorphosis prepares the individual for a pelagic-benthic transition. Upon settling onto the reef, the juvenile fish enters a period of rapid somatic expansion that culminates in the attainment of sexual maturity, an event that field surveys have linked to a specific threshold in body length. Maturation is first observed when individuals reach a standard length of approximately fifteen centimeters (15 cm) [Lp = 15 cm] measured from the snout to the posterior margin of the hypural plate, a size typically associated with the initiation of gonadal activity and the onset of vitellogenesis in females. Correspondingly, the wet weight at which this pubertal milestone is achieved has been documented at roughly sixty-five point eight grams (65.8 grams) [Wwp = 65.8 grams], derived from length-weight relationships fitted to populations harvested from the Santa Catalina Island region. These values provide a clear benchmark for the transition from the juvenile stage into the reproductively viable adult segment of the population, marking the point at which individuals begin to allocate resources toward gamete production rather than exclusively toward somatic tissue accretion.

Reproductively active adults of Hypsypops rubicundus exhibit a highly territorial, nest-guarding breeding system that is typical of the genus. Each gravid female produces approximately two hundred and nineteen eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately two hundred and nineteen eggs per clutch] and can deposit a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year] under the stable thermal conditions of seventeen point five degrees Celsius [T = seventeen point five degrees Celsius] that characterise the cool, nutrient-rich waters of the Southern California Bight during the spawning season. This annual reproductive output, while modest in comparison to some tropical damselfishes that spawn multiple times across an extended season, reflects the constraints imposed by a temperate environment with a compressed seasonal window for larval survival. The maximum lifetime reproductive rate, expressed as the total number of offspring a female can produce across her entire breeding life, reaches approximately 80,000 eggs per female over her lifespan  under those same thermal conditions. Such an overall fecundity level is facilitated by the species' iteroparous life history, which distributes reproductive effort over many consecutive years rather than concentrating it into a single explosive event.

Continued somatic growth does not cease entirely after the onset of sexual maturity; rather, the species exhibits an indeterminate growth trajectory typical of many teleosts, with body size increasing slowly but measurably throughout adult life. Field collections of the largest individuals, often nest-guarding males in prime territories, indicate that the ultimate standard length attained by Hypsypops rubicundus is approximately thirty centimeters (30 cm) [Li = 30 cm]. The corresponding ultimate wet weight associated with this maximum length has been estimated at roughly five hundred and twenty-six point five grams (526.5 grams) [Wwi = 526.5 grams], a value derived from the same species-specific length-weight conversion that provided juvenile mass estimates, placing Hypsypops rubicundus among the largest pomacentrids globally, a size advantage that likely enhances competitive success in nest-site defense. The substantial body mass achieved by terminal adults confers a distinct competitive advantage in the rocky subtidal environment, particularly during agonistic interactions over nesting substrate, where larger individuals consistently dominate access to the most favourable boulder crevices and algal-covered patches used for egg deposition and subsequent fanning.

Longevity data collected from tag-recapture programmes and otolith-based age estimation suggest that individual Hypsypops rubicundus can persist in the wild for a remarkably extended period, with the maximum recorded lifespan reaching approximately fifty-seven years [am = approximately fifty-seven years] under the prevailing thermal conditions of seventeen point five degrees Celsius [T = seventeen point five degrees Celsius]. Such extreme longevity, rivaled among pomacentrids only by certain members of the genus Stegastes in cooler temperate zones, reflects a life history strategy characterised by delayed senescence, low natural adult mortality, and consistent annual reproductive output over multiple decades. The extended lifespan permits a female to accrue the cumulative fecundity necessary to compensate for the high stochastic mortality experienced during the planktonic larval phase, ensuring that sufficient offspring survive to recruit into the adult population. Comparative data from a congeneric species, the Hawaiian dascyllus Dascyllus albisella, which possesses eggs measuring approximately seven-tenths of a millimeter in length and half a millimeter in width, provide an informative morphological baseline for scaling the reproductive investment, though the precise egg dimensions of Hypsypops rubicundus itself remain an active area of ongoing investigation.
